<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and held demand volume roughly constant, so the debate narrowed cleanly to: does redistributing the same crowd help or spread harm. Side A supplied the sharper decisive mechanisms. The nonlinear "tipping point" argument [A4.2] — that adding visitors to a block already past the residential/touristic threshold inflicts no new tipping, while spreading pushes fifty streets toward theirs — reframed "same volume, different geography" in A's favour and was never squarely rebutted; B's only answer was that leftover residents "do not count as zero," which concedes the shape of the comparison and merely disputes magnitude. A also converted B's best pressure question into a gain: the choke-point vs capillary enforcement distinction [A4.4] is a genuine, plausible reply to "why does enforcement work only as a funnel," and it simultaneously undermined B's reliance on retail rules and bed licensing holding the line across two hundred blocks. On irreversibility, A's "reputations don't expire, sunk capital lobbies to stay" beat B's "licenses expire, posters come down." B's frame ("volume says how many, geography says who pays") was memorable and forced A to state where the permitted crowd stands; A answered directly and credibly (hardened cores, transit, sanitation, staff by choice). B's strongest live thread — that containment simply elects the old-town families as the payers, and that the leak already writes an unofficial map without consent — remains partially standing, and B answered A's pressure question honestly rather than dodging ("yes, dispersal is still required; there is no sacred number"). But A then turned that concession effectively: if the cap is admittedly notional, the map is the funded policy. A's opening was clipped for length, a real execution cost, yet the case survived because the later speeches carried the load. Net: a clear but competitive win for A on the strength of the tipping-point and enforcement-scarcity comparisons.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's answer to B's Q2 in [A4.4]-[A4.5]: distinguishing checkable choke-point rules (cruise berths, bed licences) from capillary rules (keeping a bakery a bakery across two hundred blocks) neutralized the alleged contradiction and simultaneously showed B's plan requires exactly the enforcement competence the overloaded core proves is missing.</best_rebuttal>
